description:
We are a team of five hardworking members of TKS (The Knowledge Society) located in Calgary, united by our enthusiasm for space and passion for solving meaningful problems. We’re so extremely grateful for the opportunity to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge and ready to give our best effort and turn our ideas into action.

Our goal is to develop a personalized health monitor that tracks astronauts muscle deterioration and key health indicators to help them take informed action.
summary:
Astronauts lose strength in space, and exercise doesn't fully prevent it. NASA's published Mir and ISS data show average knee strength falling roughly 23-30% after flight, and future exploration systems may not support ISS-level exercise. But group averages can't tell planners whether one astronaut can still perform a spacewalk or emergency exit.

RESEARCH GAP: NASA's Human Research Roadmap identifies gap MA-102: determining the relationship between physiological and functional measures of fitness and mission-specific task performance. Related gap MA-101 covers individual variability and countermeasures.

ASTRA-FX is a browser-based prototype that aims to help fill this gap. It compares an individual's strength, endurance, fatigue, recovery, movement consistency and functional performance with their own baseline, flags persistent decline, groups it into four proposed patterns, and estimates a "Functional Reserve": the modeled margin between current capability and a mission task's demands. A What-If Lab compares hypothetical exercise strategies. The demo pairs real NASA group data with a clearly labelled synthetic subject; all metrics are illustrative, not validated.
details:
How we built it: ASTRA-FX is a static web app in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The analysis lives in a separate, transparent model file (baselines, persistence detection, decline signatures, Functional Reserve, and the what-if simulation), kept apart from the interface. Chart.js draws the charts, and Three.js renders the interactive 3D anatomy. Code was developed with AI assistance (Claude).

Data: Real NASA evidence comes from Table 5.2-3 of the NASA Human Integration Design Handbook (pre/post-flight Mir and ISS group means) and the NASA-STD-3001 in-mission strength requirement. NASA does not publish individual-level longitudinal data, so the demonstration subject is clearly labelled synthetic.

Limits: Task requirements, weights, thresholds, and exercise effect sizes are assumptions, not validated. Functional Reserve is not a NASA metric.

WHY IT'S NEEDED: In NASA's published Mir and ISS data, strength fell far more than muscle size. Knee-extension strength dropped about 23–27% while leg lean mass dropped only about 4–7%, so strength loss was roughly four to six times larger. Tracking muscle mass alone would miss most of the functional decline. And NASA's in-mission requirement is a single strength threshold (≥80% of baseline), while different mission tasks demand different things. ASTRA-FX explores how individual functional measurements could be tied to specific tasks.

Next steps: replace the synthetic subject with approved individual-level data, derive task requirements from NASA task analyses, and validate the model.

The GitHub link for this project is in "PITCH_SpaceDocs.pdf" on Google Drive.
